extracted.intended_audience: housekeepers, cooks, and home cooks preparing and preserving meats (19th-century domestic cookery)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, domestic instructions for selecting, curing, cooking, and serving various meats (beef, veal, lamb, mutton), plus related preparations (rennet, gravies, garnish). Focus is on procedures, timing, and selection to achieve best quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salting beef for preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rub salt thoroughly into every part of beef; lay fleshy side downward in tub; sprinkle abundant salt after packing; let beef lie in salt ten days, then brush off and put into brine under weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain Liverpool salt (no need for extra saltpetre initially). Let beef lie in salt ten days before brining; then about ten days in brine it will look red and be fit to eat (earlier if brine is older). Best time to begin salting is late October when weather is cool; maintain a succession of salted beef. After removal, dry the salt for next use. Tongues cured same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying beef for summer use
rubrics_metrics.description: Select thin briskets, round and rib pieces (without long ribs/back-bones); salt, let lie a fortnight, then brine for three weeks, wipe dry, rub with bran and hang in cool, dry, dark place suspended so pieces do not touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces should come from animals well-fattened with corn (~150 lb per quarter). Inspect occasionally through summer; after long wet spells, lay in sun a few hours. Dried meats must be soaked overnight before use and boiled gently in plenty of cold water, skimming until bones fall out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curing with saltpetre and molasses (hot-weather corned beef)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rub both sides of thin brisket with pounded saltpetre, pour on molasses and salt and rub in; keep in a vessel not airtight so bloody brine can drain; cover with molasses and salt and after four days boil tied in cloth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vessel just large enough but not tight. Best stored in ice-house or refrigerator if available. Same method works for fillet of veal and mutton leg/rack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting meat by fat and grain
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose butchers' meat by fat color (not yellow) and by fine close-grained lean with lively color and tender feel when pinched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject beef fat with high yellow shade and any tinge of yellow in veal, mutton, lamb, or pork. Poultry should have white fat and a gristly (not hard) bottom of breast bone indicates youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roasting general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not run the spit through delicate parts; soak piece in water 1 hour, wash, dry, then set before a clear steady fire; baste initially with salt/water then with nice lard in the dripping-pan, and when near done cover with paper then remove and dredge with flour and baste to raise a froth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lard rather than butter for basting roasted meats. When meat has been down some time but before browning, cover with paper and baste; when nearly done remove paper, dredge with flour and baste rapidly to 'froth' the surface. Beef and mutton should be roasted less than veal, lamb, or pork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roasting requires a spit and jack
rubrics_metrics.description: No meat can be well roasted except on a spit turned by a jack before a steady clear fire; other methods are similar to baking and inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid half-boiling meats before spitting (it destroys flavor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling meats from cold water with salt
rubrics_metrics.description: Put foods to be boiled into cold water with a little salt so they cook evenly; if put into boiling water the outside overcooks before inside heats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When boiling for stews or soups, use plenty of water and boil steadily, skimming frequently until bones are ready to fall out (or until skin peels off for tongue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frying and choice of fat
rubrics_metrics.description: Nice lard is superior to butter for basting roasted meats or for frying; for broiling use clear coals; dredge items with flour or meal mixed with salt before frying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay items on a board to dry after dredging; when one side is dry turn and dredge the other. Drain fried items on a strainer to remove grease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broiling and grilling guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For broiling have very clear coals, sprinkle a little salt and pepper; after broiling, pour over melted butter and chopped parsley for veal, wild fowl, birds or poultry; beef-steaks and mutton chops need only a spoonful of hot water poured over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For steaks, rub the gridiron bars with a cloth dipped in lard before heating so drippings do not cause bad smell. Every thing must be ready — steaks are best served immediately from the gridiron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steak selection and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Best part for beef-steaks is the seventh and eighth ribs; cut steaks half an inch thick and beat them a little before broiling; do not salt until you dish them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broil quick, turn frequently; dish on very hot dish, add some onion slices, sprinkle a little salt, pour over a spoonful each of hot water and mushroom catsup, garnish with horse-radish, and cover with a hot dish cover so steam rises when uncovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thickness and timing for cutlets and chops
rubrics_metrics.description: Veal cutlets and chops are cut about half an inch thick (cutlets from fillet or leg); beat them, coat with egg and bread crumbs, dry so crumbs adhere, and fry in boiling lard until light brown then stew in seasoned gravy for 15–20 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double coating (egg, crumbs), press crumbs on, and drain cutlets thoroughly; prepare gravy with curry powder, wine, lemon pickle and thicken with butter and brown flour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stewing and fricando methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Brown or lard slices, then stew in well-seasoned gravy until tender; add vegetables like sorrel or spinach or serve with stewed vegetables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include fricando of beef and veal a-la-daube: layer beef with bacon and herbs, cover with water, stew gently, strain and clarify gravy with beaten egg whites and water if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larding and forcemeat stuffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Make forcemeats from bread crumbs, marrow or fat bacon, herbs and spices mixed with egg yolks; stuff rounds or fill hollows created by removing bones; lard tops with strips of bacon and sew or bind to keep compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie or fillet with linen to maintain shape before roasting or baking; garnish with forcemeat balls fried. When boiling stuffed joints, simmer gently for many hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using paper to preserve moisture in roasting
rubrics_metrics.description: When roasting, cover meats with paper during much of the cooking to retain moisture; remove paper near end to brown and froth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let paper burn — use buttered paper when wrapping chops for broiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gravy preparation (brown gravy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a supply of brown flour (toast flour to a uniform dark brown but do not burn) to thicken brown gravies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toast a pint of flour in a Dutch oven over coals, constantly stirring until uniformly dark brown. Thicken gravies with this and with butter rubbed into flour; strain and skim fat as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carving and serving presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint items at their separations so they can be neatly carved at table; dish certain cuts (loin of veal, hind quarter of lamb) with kidneys uppermost; serve meats hot, on hot dishes, with appropriate garnishes (horse-radish for beef/mutton, mint for lamb, white sauce for veal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dinner is more elegant when consisting mostly of small, well-prepared articles neatly served; keep dishes hot by setting over hot water or putting something hot in them, and cover with pewter dish cover until served.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition/age of animal for best meat
rubrics_metrics.description: Best age for beef is 3 to 5 years; older or diseased animals cause meat to shrink when cooked (not lunar phase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient prejudice about moon phase is dismissed; shrinking is due to age or disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying diseased meat by fat color
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject meat with yellow-tinged fat; healthy fat should be white (or not high shade of yellow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jewish butchers historically paid to remove diseased meat; use fat color as a practical rule for beef, veal, mutton, lamb, pork, and poultry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing fish for frying
rubrics_metrics.description: After preparing fish, lay on board and dredge with flour or meal mixed with salt; when one side dries, turn and dredge the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broiling fish use clear coals; after broiling, pour melted butter and chopped parsley for veal and birds; beef steaks require only hot water poured over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashing and reusing cooked meats
rubrics_metrics.description: Hash uses slices of raw or cooked meat stewed briefly with a prepared gravy; if using cooked meat, have a gravy already prepared and keep the hash on the fire only a few minutes to heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thicken with butter rubbed into brown flour; use garlic, catsup, and seasonings as preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pies and enclosed dishes
rubrics_metrics.description: For meat pies (e.g., beef steak pie, sweetbreads and oysters pie), partially cook fillings as required, place in pastry (puff paste or deep dish with paste sides but no bottom), cover with top paste and bake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sweetbreads with oysters: thicken with cream, butter, egg yolks and flour; this makes a delicate pie. For mock turtle or calf's head pies reduce gravy to desired strength before filling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and use of rennet
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove calf stomach immediately after slaughter; do not wash, hang in cool dry place 4–5 days, turn inside out and scrape off curd, salt with saltpetre and salt, add small vinegar and cover; after 6–8 weeks cut a piece and macerate in cold water and rose brandy to use (1 dessertspoonful per quart milk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not wash (weakens gastric juice). Prepare in very cool weather; keeps more than a year if well done. Use one tablespoonful of prepared rennet for a quart of milk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning calf's head and feet
rubrics_metrics.description: After slaughter, remove head and feet, sprinkle pounded rosin over hairs, dip in boiling water then scrape quickly; soak feet in water 3–4 days changing water daily to whiten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rosin dries immediately and facilitates scraping; appropriate for country households who butcher their own animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific cuts recommended for particular cooking methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cuts are recommended for different preparations: loin of veal always roasted; fillet/leg may be roasted or various; knuckle/knee for soup or boiling; fore-quarter (shoulder, neck) mainly for soup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For steaks, 7th and 8th ribs best; thin briskets/plate for drying; brisket, round and rib pieces for drying and preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasoning and aromatic use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use garlic, thyme, parsley, nutmeg, cloves, mace, pepper, salt, lemon pickle, wine, mushroom and walnut catsup, capers, and curry powder in various combinations to season gravies and dishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: curry powder + wine + lemon pickle for veal cutlet gravy; garlic and red wine for baked brisket; caper sauce for mutton grill; mushroom/walnut catsup commonly used to flavor gravies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skimming and clarifying gravies
rubrics_metrics.description: Skim fat from gravies and, to clarify strong gravies, beat whites of eggs with water and add to gravy, boil until clear and strain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skimming and removing grease improves flavor and appearance; remove fat before bottling gravies for use as seasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binding, shaping and pressing boiled joints
rubrics_metrics.description: After boiling stuffed or bandaged joints, cool under boards with weight for 24 hours, then remove bandages and cut thin slices from ends; keep some items covered in vinegar and water for preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: collaring a flank of beef — after boiling, press under weight; collaring calf's head — bind, boil half hour and press; keep covered with vinegar and water for serving later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of heat and gentle stewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jointed or tough cuts should be stewed or boiled gently for long periods (5–6 hours for some), not boiled violently, to attain tenderness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stewing in gravy, simmer gently until tender, then skim and thicken gravy and garnish appropriately; for some baked items, 3–5 hours in an oven is recommended (e.g., beef a-la-mode, brisket).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid visible dry flour on roasted meats
rubrics_metrics.description: When dredging with flour and frothing, ensure no particle of dry flour remains visible on the meat as it looks ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper basting and frothing will incorporate the flour into the surface sauce; when mutton and beef are properly roasted they may look brown but other meats should be paler.
